doc.title: Bill Dobbins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rochester, New York, January 11, 2012

title: Myths of talent and Charlie Parker's practicing
summary: Dobbins plays students a Paul Desmond interview with Parker about practicing ten or eleven hours a day.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Oh yeah. And in relation to jazz education, one of the things that I deal with even with jazz majors let alone with people that are not musicians or that don’t play jazz, is they still want to believe this myth that certain people are just anointed from above or that if you just ingest the right substance or hang out with the masters, you know, that this stuff is going to rub off. And they even sometimes fall prey to these myths because it’s a more attractive story. It’s the more fun thing to believe. It just takes a lot of hard work. One of the things that — I was fortunate to get it just a couple of years ago that I’ve been playing for my students at least once in every class, Gary Foster, who’s been a good friend of mine for many years, I think he got these from Warne Marsh, one of the few recorded interviews with Charlie Parker. And there’s one of them, my favorite, is an interview that Paul Desmond did with Charlie Parker for this radio show.
I think I just saw it recently.

Yeah. It’s just amazing. And I mean one of the things that — well after listening to this one cut, Paul Desmond mentions that he noticed in the Parker solo that he quoted — used this pattern from the Klosé Etude book you know. And he said you know a lot of people think that this amazing facility that you have on the saxophone and this amazing facility with the language of improvisation and that’s just something that you are born with and it’s just sort of natural. He said — I heard this quote from the study and I was just wondering if you always did a lot of serious practicing. And then Parker says, very specifically he says, yeah from the time I was living at home and going to school, there was a period around the time that I was eleven, maybe six or seven years where I practiced ten, eleven hours a day. He said I practiced so much that the landlord was constantly threatening to evict us from the apartment. He said, “I was giving my mother problems.” So Desmond said, “That’s comforting to hear about it.” It just wasn’t done just with smoke and mirrors. He said, “No it wasn’t done with smoke and mirrors, it was done with books.”
